candidates.title: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock
candidates.author: Airbnb engineers with AWS (AWS ML blog)
candidates.what_changed: Airbnb publishes its operating method for internal coding agents (AirChat): eval-measured cost per task drives model defaults and gateway-enforced reasoning-effort ceilings, then production CloudWatch/gateway telemetry is compared against eval expectations.
candidates.mechanism: Cost per task = list-price cost of all four token classes (uncached input, cache read, cache write, output) summed over every request in a task. Seven eval suites in Harbor format (instruction.md, task.toml, Dockerfile, grader, reference solution); 8-dimension weighted model-graded rubric with a ceiling (autonomy 0/0.5 caps score at 25/100). Derived OTPS = OutputTokenCount/(InvocationLatency-TimeToFirstToken)*1000. Explains Bedrock TPM quota reservation (uncached input + cache writes + max_tokens reserved up front; cache reads never count; output burndown multipliers).
candidates.evidence_quality: Practitioner-measured production data from a named customer, published on vendor (AWS) blog; figures are relative (no absolute dollars).
candidates.relevance: Very high: concrete, reusable recipe for coding-agent cost governance, eval-to-production comparison, latency triage and throttling diagnosis.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Thematic overlap with Ed2 TokenEconomizer and Databricks AI Index (coding-agent tokenomics) but different, operational angle; new.
candidates.summary: Thousands of Airbnb engineers use AirChat weekly; all requests route through an LLM gateway on Bedrock. Eight new models shipped in ~5 weeks; by mid-October ~2/3 of coding-agent requests went to those new models. On one model, low->high reasoning effort raised score by 0.8 points but cost per task 2.5x, so effort ceilings are gateway-enforced. New-model eval campaigns produce first results within hours and full suite scores + cost per task by next morning. Key cautionary tale: 'model A' scored >3 points above the prior best at about the same eval cost per task, but in production weekly spend per user was several times higher: each request cost ~3x and users sent ~3x as many requests, because long self-directed sessions re-read cached context (output tokens were only ~1/10 of request cost). A newer model scoring higher at ~1/6 the cost per task replaced it via config change; the heavy-user group's spend on their main model fell to ~1/7 in the first full week with similar request counts. Latency case: latency +40% with flat TTFT and OTPS was traced to a system-prompt change that raised output tokens per request 50% - treat prompt changes and model upgrades as deploys. Prereqs: invocation logging (off by default; holds full prompts), tagged IAM roles with cost-allocation tags activated before collection (no backfill), dated list-price table.

candidates.title: LangSmith for Coding Agents: Now track spend by outcome
candidates.author: Jacob Lee
candidates.what_changed: LangSmith adds a 'coding agent' agent type (public beta, LangSmith Cloud) that attributes trace spend to GitHub PRs / GitLab MRs ('outcomes').
candidates.mechanism: Plugins for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Deep Agents send traces; GitHub connection links threads to PRs (many-to-many: one thread can open several PRs, one PR can take several threads). Dashboard: cost per PR by state (open/closed/merged), unattributed spend (no PR), work-type labelling (feature/bug fix/investigation/review/off-topic), skill-call usage, most expensive PRs, cost vs thread length.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor product announcement; no measured customer results. Cites $34B 2026 enterprise coding spend figure without source detail.
candidates.independent_confirmation: LangSmith docs page (docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agents) describes the coding agent type as beta (via WebSearch); Digg summary.
candidates.relevance: High: directly addresses 'what does our coding-agent spend buy'; pairs naturally with Airbnb cost-per-task story.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Distinct from previously seen LangSmith trace controls (Nov 17) and proactive agents posts.
candidates.summary: Setup is three steps: install the LangSmith plugin per agent (Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add langchain-ai/langsmith-claude-code-plugins; /plugin install langsmith-tracing@langsmith-claude-code-plugins; /reload-plugins), connect GitHub, open the coding agent overview. Suggested uses: compare cost per merged PR before/after a model switch; measure savings from moving subagents to smaller models; find skills that appear in long expensive threads (rewrite candidates) vs short threads ending in merges; coach on long threads, since every turn re-carries full context. Traces count toward normal LangSmith tracing usage. LangChain notes its own coding agent Robin's rising spend motivated the feature and its model router.

candidates.title: LangSmith Tool Gateway: Secure, governed tool use for agents
candidates.author: Karthic Subramanian
candidates.what_changed: Public beta of a managed MCP tool layer in LangSmith that handles credentials, identity, per-agent tool scoping, deny/approval policies and tool-call tracing; complements existing LLM Gateway.
candidates.mechanism: Register MCP servers by URL or enable built-ins (Google, Microsoft, Salesforce, GitHub, Linear, LinkedIn via LangSmith-run OAuth; API-key tools such as Exa, Tavily, Parallel). Bundle tools into 'tool kits' exposed at one MCP URL; 'search mode' loads only relevant tools for large kits. Identity: act-as-user (IdP like Okta/Entra; first call returns sign-in link then resumes) or act-as-agent (agent auth or shared 'profiles'). Deny policies per user/service key/org/workspace; approval policies require human confirmation in the MCP client. Traces record tool, server, user, outcome, latency but not payloads; Enterprise audit log records which tool ran as whom.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor product announcement; anecdotal customer example (US retailer with 50+ MCP servers, >1,000 tools) without outcome metrics.
candidates.relevance: High: practical pattern for agent tool governance (scoping, on-behalf-of auth, HITL approvals, audit). Works with any MCP client incl. Claude Code and Cursor.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Same theme as AWS AgentCore Gateway/Skyflow and BMW governance posts this window; could be clustered as 'tool-call governance moves to gateways'.
candidates.summary: Problem framing: production agents serve thousands of users each with their own permissions; hard-coding OAuth per provider and handing agents whole tool servers gives no deterministic check against wrong credentials or unapproved tools. Example: retailer store-assistant agent acting with each associate's credentials vs 3 a.m. inventory agent using service credentials, each limited to a small subset of >1,000 tools. Five-step setup: open Tools, add server, connect account, build kit, point client at kit URL.

candidates.title: Why agent governance starts with observability
candidates.author: Christine Manegan
candidates.what_changed: Framework essay: preventative vs detective governance, both dependent on tracing.
candidates.mechanism: Preventative = runtime guardrails, identity, tool/model/cost policies, pre-production eval gates; detective = online evals, alerts, drift detection, human review; detective findings feed back into guardrails and regression tests.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor opinion/marketing; no data.
candidates.relevance: Low-medium; useful framing only, companion to Tool Gateway launch.
candidates.summary: Cites OWASP Agentic AI Threats & Mitigations, NIST AI RMF and EU law as guidance that lists risks but not verification. Example pre-deploy gates: <2% hallucination, no PII leakage, >90% correctness vs human labels on a golden dataset. Argues guardrails must be verified continuously through traces/trajectories.

candidates.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks
candidates.author: AWS
candidates.what_changed: AgentCore's managed harness now runs on open-source Strands harness (Apache 2.0) with managed defaults and adds four lifecycle hook points.
candidates.mechanism: Defaults: evolving recommended model, task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially Anthropic models via Converse), proactive context summarization at configurable threshold, context offloading of large tool results (preview + retrieve), todo_write planning that survives summarization, subagent delegation tool, web_fetch, separate read/write/edit filesystem tools. Hooks: before_invocation, before_tool_call (Lambda deny skips the tool call, loop continues), after_tool_call, after_invocation; only Lambda hooks can block, SNS/EventBridge are notify-only. Sessions run in kernel-isolated microVMs.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor claim; '~34% lower token cost than other leading harnesses' is unsubstantiated in the post.
candidates.relevance: High for builders on AWS: deterministic allow/deny at tool-call boundary; warning that allowedTools omitted or ['*'] means the tool set can grow over time, so fixed security boundaries should enumerate tools.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Different from previously seen AgentCore JSON workloads post (Nov 17).
candidates.summary: No new resource type; existing harnesses get the upgrade automatically. Explicit model ID, systemPrompt, truncation policy and allowedTools override managed defaults. Example: refund approval limit checked by a before_tool_call Lambda. Example minimal config {"allowedTools": ["read","web_fetch"]} gives read-only FS + web retrieval with no shell.

candidates.title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture's sequenced approach
candidates.author: AWS and Accenture
candidates.what_changed: Six-lever, three-phase token-cost playbook with four anonymized client results.
candidates.mechanism: Attribution first (application inference profiles + cost allocation tags, CUR 2.0, invocation logging; Accenture 'Cost per Business Transaction' incl. retries and failed attempts). Phase 1 config: prompt caching (up to 90% off cached input), batch inference (50% off). Phase 2 architecture: intelligent prompt routing (up to 30%), RAG tuning, context scoping/compression. Phase 3: semantic caching, distillation.
candidates.evidence_quality: Consultancy/vendor-reported client results, anonymized, levers often combined so not separable.
candidates.relevance: Medium-high: cost playbook with numbers; recommends one lever at a time with held-out production-derived evals.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Overlaps with Ed2 tokenomics theme (Databricks AI Index, TokenEconomizer); mentions new Linux Foundation 'Tokenomics Foundation' (UNVERIFIED beyond this post).
candidates.summary: Results: large enterprise (all-frontier, no caching) -85% monthly token cost via tiering+caching+batch, ~15% of tasks still needed top model; telecom $12M/yr -> $3.8M (-68%), input tokens -70% via triage routing, semantic cache, context compression; insurer (prefix caching) and miner (semantic cache) ~40% combined. Semantic cache benchmark cited: 63,796 real chatbot queries, 0.90 threshold -> 74.5% hit rate, 92.3% accuracy, 72.5% savings. Distillation claim: up to 500% faster, 75% cheaper, <2% accuracy loss (AWS claim).

candidates.title: How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers
candidates.author: BMW Group with AWS
candidates.what_changed: Enterprise practitioner write-up of agent governance patterns codified as IaC.
candidates.mechanism: Governance externalized to integration layer (MCP gateway, central agent registry); graduated per-step autonomy levels 0 (HITL), 1 (human-on-the-loop), 2 (autonomous within deterministic guardrails); policy-as-code gates in CI/CD; egress controls (recipient allowlisting, outbound secret scanning); OpenTelemetry intent tracing; verification tests gate evaluation runs; ground-truth dataset required before implementation.
candidates.evidence_quality: Practitioner experience; scale figures but no outcome metrics.
candidates.relevance: Medium-high: concrete governance checklist from regulated large org.
candidates.summary: Context: 12,500+ R&D developers, ~500M lines of vehicle software, 1,300+ backend microservices serving 24M vehicles; building agents since 2023. Five practices; key advice: assign trust levels per step not per agent; agents lacking instrumentation fail CI validation; capture model-routing decisions and justification; five pre-build artifacts (scope, interaction model, tool definitions, ground-truth dataset, eval criteria).

candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor/partner solution post; no measured results.

candidates.title: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say
candidates.author: Bruno Duarte et al. (Dharma-AI)
candidates.what_changed: Preview of paper showing learned predictor of end-to-end SFT job duration vastly beats 6PD FLOP estimate.
